drills.title: Total revenue from CSV text
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines (and indent them) so the function adds up quantity times unit price for every row of the CSV text. io.StringIO makes a string behave like an opened file. Two lines do not belong. The two imports can go in either order.
drills.explain: DictReader needs something that behaves like an open file, so a plain string must be wrapped (io.StringIO(text)); given a bare string it would loop over single characters. Every value read from a CSV is text, so quantity and unit_price must go through int() before the multiplication. The return sits outside the loop, at the same level as the for, so it runs after all rows are added.

drills.title: Save and load settings as JSON
drills.prompt: Fill the two blanks. io.StringIO() is an in-memory file, so json.dump can write to it and getvalue() returns the text that was written. The program then turns that text back into a dict.
drills.explain: The names without an s work with files: dump(obj, file) writes JSON into a file, load(file) reads it back. The names with an s work with strings: dumps(obj) returns text and loads(text) parses text. Here we write into a file-like object (dump) and then parse a string (loads). The "s" stands for string.

drills.title: Everything in a CSV is text
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
code: print(sum(int(r["qty"]) * int(r["price"]) for r in rows))
drills.explain: DictReader turns each row into a dict keyed by the header, and every value is a str, even the digits (note the quotes around '2' and '30'). Multiplying the text "2" by 2 repeats it: 22. Convert with int() first and you get the number 4. The last line converts both columns before multiplying: 2 * 30 + 3 * 50.

drills.title: load or loads?
drills.prompt: The program stops with an AttributeError. Click the faulty line and choose the fix.
drills.explain: json.load expects an open file and calls .read() on it. A str has no read method, hence the AttributeError. For text already in a variable use json.loads (the s is for string). dumps would go in the opposite direction and give you more text, and json has no parse function.

drills.title: Review the AI's region report
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this report from CSV sales data. It runs and prints something plausible, but tick the statements that point at real problems.

issues.text: Each region keeps only its LAST order instead of the total (North shows 5997, not 9995)
issues.why: The assignment replaces the old value. Use the group-and-total pattern: revenue_by_region[region] = revenue_by_region.get(region, 0) + revenue.

issues.text: str(revenue_by_region) writes Python text with single quotes, which is not valid JSON
issues.why: A JSON reader would reject {'North': 5997}. Use json.dump(revenue_by_region, out) (or json.dumps) so the result is real JSON with double quotes.

non_issues.text: int(row["quantity"]) is unnecessary because the CSV already has numbers
non_issues.why: DictReader returns text for every cell. The int() calls are exactly what is needed before doing maths.
DictReader accepts any file-like object, and StringIO is an in-memory file. With a real file you would use open(..., newline="") instead.

non_issues.text: list(csv.DictReader(...)) is wrong because the reader is a list already
non_issues.why: DictReader is an iterator that can be read only once. list() collects the rows so they can be reused.

drills.explain: Report code often looks right because it prints numbers. Check two things when you review it: does a group-and-total loop add to the previous value, and does the output format match what the next reader (a JSON or CSV parser) expects?
